1

SL Recap

Reconfirm the core retrieval and join skills before moving into aggregates.

Syntax reference — SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, multi-table JOIN, LIKE 
-- Filter rows and sort the result
SELECT column_a, column_b
FROM table_name
WHERE level_column = 'HL'
ORDER BY category_column, name_column;

-- Two-table join
SELECT a.name_column, b.group_name, a.value_column
FROM first_table AS a
INNER JOIN second_table AS b
    ON a.group_id = b.group_id;

-- Three-table join
SELECT a.name_column, c.title_column, b.value_column
FROM link_table   AS b
INNER JOIN first_table  AS a ON b.first_id = a.first_id
INNER JOIN second_table AS c ON b.second_id = c.second_id
WHERE b.period_column = 'Spring';

-- LIKE searches a text column for a pattern
SELECT name_column
FROM table_name
WHERE name_column LIKE '%text%';

Aliases such as a, b, and c shorten long queries. When several tables contain similarly named columns, qualify them with the alias to avoid ambiguity.

2

Aggregate Functions and Grouping

Build reporting queries that summarize grouped data.

Syntax reference — COUNT, AVG, SUM, MAX, MIN, GROUP BY, HAVING 
-- Count rows in each group
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;

-- Average a numeric value in each group
SELECT group_column, ROUND(AVG(score_column), 1) AS average_score
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;

-- MAX and MIN find the largest and smallest value in each group
SELECT group_column,
       MAX(score_column) AS highest_score,
       MIN(score_column) AS lowest_score
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;

-- SUM totals a numeric column for each group
SELECT category_column, SUM(number_column) AS total_value
FROM table_name
GROUP BY category_column;

-- HAVING filters groups after aggregation
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4;

Key rule: WHERE filters rows before grouping, while HAVING filters grouped results after the aggregate functions have run. Non-aggregated columns in the SELECT list must appear in GROUP BY.

3

Views

Create a reusable query layer on top of the base tables.

Syntax reference — CREATE VIEW and querying views 
-- Create a view from a reusable SELECT query
CREATE VIEW view_name AS
SELECT column_a, column_b, column_c
FROM table_name
WHERE status_column = 'Active';

-- Query a view just like a table
SELECT *
FROM view_name
ORDER BY column_a;

-- Drop a view definition
DROP VIEW view_name;

A virtual view stores the query definition, not the result rows themselves. You can query it like a table, but the underlying SELECT runs each time unless the database supports materialized views or snapshots.

  1. A3.3.5 CREATE VIEW

  3. A3.3.5 Explain

4

Transactions and ACID

Use transaction control language to protect data integrity.

Syntax reference — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK 
-- Start a transaction
BEGIN;

UPDATE account_table
SET balance_column = balance_column - 50
WHERE account_id = 1;

UPDATE account_table
SET balance_column = balance_column + 50
WHERE account_id = 2;

COMMIT; -- makes the whole transaction permanent

-- Undo an uncommitted transaction
BEGIN;

UPDATE table_name
SET status_column = 'Archived'
WHERE id_column = 10;

ROLLBACK; -- returns the data to its state before BEGIN

ACID reminder: Atomicity means all of the transaction succeeds or none of it does. Consistency, Isolation, and Durability are what make transactions reliable under real use.

  1. A3.3.6 BEGIN / COMMIT

    Begin a transaction, insert a new student, insert one matching enrollment row for that student, then commit the transaction.

  2. A3.3.6 BEGIN / ROLLBACK

    Begin a second transaction, make a change to a score or cohort, inspect the result, then roll the transaction back.

  3. A3.3.6 ACID

Model Answers — Course Enrolment

Section 1 — SL Recap

1
Composite key in ENROLLMENT The composite key is (StudentID, CourseID). It represents the real-world fact that one student enrolls in one course — the combination is unique per enrolment row.
2 
SELECT * FROM COURSE
WHERE Level = 'HL'
ORDER BY Department, CourseName;
3 
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Cohort = 2026;
4 
SELECT c.CourseName, d.DepartmentName, c.Credits
FROM COURSE c
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON c.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID;
5 
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, c.CourseName, e.Score
FROM ENROLLMENT e
INNER JOIN STUDENT s ON e.StudentID = s.StudentID
INNER JOIN COURSE  c ON e.CourseID  = c.CourseID
WHERE e.Semester = 'Spring';
6 
SELECT CourseName FROM COURSE
WHERE CourseName LIKE '%Design%' OR CourseName LIKE '%Analytics%';

Section 2 — Aggregate Functions and Grouping

1 
SELECT DepartmentID, COUNT(*) AS CourseCount
FROM COURSE
GROUP BY DepartmentID;
2 
SELECT CourseID, COUNT(*) AS EnrolmentCount
FROM ENROLLMENT
GROUP BY CourseID;
3 
SELECT d.DepartmentName, ROUND(AVG(e.Score), 1) AS AvgScore
FROM ENROLLMENT e
INNER JOIN COURSE     c ON e.CourseID     = c.CourseID
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON c.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID
GROUP BY d.DepartmentName;
4 
SELECT CourseID, MAX(Score) AS Highest, MIN(Score) AS Lowest
FROM ENROLLMENT
GROUP BY CourseID;
5 
SELECT Level, SUM(Credits) AS TotalCredits
FROM COURSE
GROUP BY Level;
6 
SELECT d.DepartmentName, COUNT(*) AS Enrolments
FROM ENROLLMENT e
INNER JOIN COURSE     c ON e.CourseID     = c.CourseID
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON c.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID
GROUP BY d.DepartmentName
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4;
7 
SELECT CourseID, AVG(Score) AS AvgScore
FROM ENROLLMENT
GROUP BY CourseID
HAVING AVG(Score) > 85;
8 
SELECT d.DepartmentName,
       COUNT(*)              AS Enrolments,
       ROUND(AVG(e.Score),1) AS AvgScore
FROM ENROLLMENT e
INNER JOIN COURSE     c ON e.CourseID     = c.CourseID
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON c.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID
GROUP BY d.DepartmentName
ORDER BY AvgScore DESC;

Section 3 — Views

1 
CREATE VIEW HighScorers AS
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName,
       c.CourseName, d.DepartmentName, e.Score
FROM ENROLLMENT e
INNER JOIN STUDENT    s ON e.StudentID    = s.StudentID
INNER JOIN COURSE     c ON e.CourseID     = c.CourseID
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON c.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID
WHERE e.Score >= 90;
2 
SELECT * FROM HighScorers
ORDER BY Score DESC, LastName;
3
Virtual vs materialized view Benefit of a virtual view: it always reflects current data — when base tables change, the next query of the view shows updated results. Difference: a materialized view stores a physical copy of the query result, making reads much faster but requiring explicit refresh commands to stay current. A virtual view uses no extra storage but re-executes the full join on every access.

Section 4 — Transactions and ACID

1 
BEGIN;

INSERT INTO STUDENT (StudentID, FirstName, LastName, Cohort)
VALUES (999, 'Alex', 'Chen', 2026);

INSERT INTO ENROLLMENT (StudentID, CourseID, Semester, Score)
VALUES (999, 101, 'Spring', 78);

COMMIT;
2 
BEGIN;

UPDATE ENROLLMENT SET Score = 100 WHERE StudentID = 999;
SELECT Score FROM ENROLLMENT WHERE StudentID = 999;

ROLLBACK;
3
ACID explanation Atomicity: if the student INSERT succeeds but the ENROLLMENT INSERT fails (e.g. constraint violation), both changes roll back — no orphaned student record. Consistency: foreign key constraints always hold; no enrollment can reference a non-existent student. Isolation: two simultaneous enrollment processes do not see each other's uncommitted changes, preventing double-booking. Durability: once COMMIT is issued, the data is written to persistent storage and survives a power failure.

Section 5 — Normalization and Denormalization Review

1
3NF advantage In the normalized design, student name is stored once in STUDENT; course name and credits once in COURSE. A flat table repeating these on every enrollment row would contain transitive dependencies — e.g. DepartmentOffice depends on DepartmentID which depends on CourseID, not on the primary key (StudentID, CourseID). 3NF removes those transitive dependencies.
2
Partial dependency If the table stored StudentFirstName alongside the composite key (StudentID, CourseID), StudentFirstName depends only on StudentID — not on the full composite key. This partial dependency violates 2NF and causes the student's name to be repeated once per enrolled course, creating update anomalies.
3
Denormalized dashboard table A ENROLMENT_REPORT table could store: DepartmentName, CourseName, Level, StudentName, Semester, Score. Benefit: the BI dashboard reads one flat table with no joins. Tradeoff: if a department is renamed, every row must be updated; if not, reports show the old name — introducing inconsistency. Update anomalies from non-3NF design reappear.
